'''''Spiraea''''' {{IPAc-en|s|p|aɪ|ˈ|r|iː|ə}},<ref>''Sunset Western Garden Book''. 1995. 606–07.</ref> sometimes spelled '''spirea''' in common names, and commonly known as '''meadowsweets''' or '''steeplebushes''', is a genus of about 80 to 100 species<ref name=china>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=131015 ''Spiraea''.] Flora of China.</ref> of [[shrub]]s in the family [[Rosaceae]]. They are native to the temperate [[Northern Hemisphere]], with the greatest diversity in eastern Asia.

The genus formerly included the herbaceous species now [[segregate (taxonomy)|segregated]] into the genera ''[[Filipendula]]'' and ''[[Aruncus]]''; recent [[genetics|genetic]] evidence has shown that ''Filipendula'' is only distantly related to ''Spiraea'', belonging in the subfamily [[Rosoideae]].

==Description==
[[File:Spiraea hypericifolia flowerdiagram.png|thumb|right|[[Flower#Floral formula|Flower diagram]] of ''[[Spiraea hypericifolia]]'']]
[[image:Spiraea betulifolia (5087436129).jpg|thumb|right|''[[Spiraea betulifolia]]'']]
[[File:Spiraea japonica 'Goldflame' 06.jpg|thumb|''[[Spiraea japonica]]'' 'Goldflame' 06]]
[[image:Autumn ball.JPG|thumb|right|''[[Spiraea betulifolia]]'' in autumn]]
''Spiraea'' plants are [[wikt:hardy|hardy]], deciduous-leaved [[shrub]]s. The [[leaf|leaves]] are simple and usually short stalked, and are [[phyllotaxis|arranged]] in a spiralling, alternate fashion. In most species, the leaves are [[lanceolate]] (narrowly oval) and about {{convert|2.5|to|10|cm|in}} long. The leaf margins are usually toothed, occasionally cut or lobed, and rarely smooth. [[Stipule]]s are absent.

The many small [[flower]]s of ''Spiraea'' shrubs are clustered together in [[inflorescence]]s, usually in dense [[panicle]]s, umbrella-like [[corymb]]s, or grape-like clusters. The [[radial symmetry]] of each flower is fivefold, with the [[flower]]s usually bisexual, rarely unisexual. The flowers have five [[sepals]] and five white, pink, or reddish [[petals]] that are usually longer than the sepals. Each flower has many (15 to 60) [[stamens]]. The fruit is an [[aggregate fruit|aggregate]] of [[Follicle (fruit)|follicle]]s.<ref name=china/>

==Ecology==
''Spiraea'' species are used as food plants by the [[larva]]e of many [[Lepidoptera]] species, including the [[brown-tail]], the [[Saturnia pavonia|small emperor moth]], the [[grey dagger]], the [[setaceous Hebrew character]], and the moth ''[[Hypercompe indecisa]]''.

The leaves of ''[[Spiraea betulifolia|S. betulifolia]]'' are eaten by [[blue grouse]] in spring, and the plant is browsed by deer in summer.<ref>{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/437 437] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/437 }}</ref>

==Uses==

=== Food ===
[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] ate the species ''S. betulifolia''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Reiner |first=Ralph E. |title=Introducing the Flowering Beauty of Glacier National Park and the Majestic High Rockies |publisher=Glacier Park, Inc. |year=1969 |pages=20 }}</ref>

===Horticulture===
[[Image:Spiraea japonica.jpg|thumb|right|''[[Spiraea japonica]]'']]
Many species of ''Spiraea'' are used as [[ornamental plant]]s in temperate climates, particularly for their showy clusters of dense flowers. Some species bloom in the spring, others in midsummer.

===Traditional medicine===
''Spiraea'' contain [[Salicylic acid|salicylates]]. [[aspirin|Acetylsalicylic acid]] was first isolated from ''[[Filipendula ulmaria]]'',<ref>Bandurska H. 2013. Salicylic acid: an update on biosynthesis and action in plant response to water deficit and performance under drought. In: ''Salicylic acid'' (pp. 1–14). Springer, Dordrecht</ref> a species at the time classified in the genus ''Spiraea''. The word "aspirin" was coined by adding ''a-'' (for [[acetylation]]) to ''spirin'', from the German ''Spirsäure'', a reference to ''Spiraea''.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/978-1-84628-933-0_3.pdf#page-1 |doi=10.1007/978-1-84628-933-0_3 |chapter=Symptomatic drug treatment |title=Inflammatory Arthritis in Clinical Practice |year=2007 |last1=Scott |first1=David L. |last2=Kingsley |first2=Gabrielle H. |pages=48–64 |isbn=978-1-84628-932-3 }}</ref><ref>Harper, D. [http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=aspirin aspirin.] Online Etymology Dictionary. 2013.</ref><ref>Weiss, H. J. (1974). [http://jama.jamanetwork.com/article.aspx?articleid=356473 Aspirin – A dangerous drug?] ''JAMA'' 229(9), 1221-22.</ref>

Native American groups have various medicinal uses for local ''Spiraea'' species. ''S. betulifolia'' is used for abdominal pain and made into a tea.<ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Spiraea+betulifolia ''Spiraea betulifolia''.] Native American Ethnobotany. University of Michigan, Dearborn.</ref> The [[Blackfoot Confederacy|Blackfoot]] use ''S. splendens'' root in an [[enema]] and to treat [[sex organ|venereal]] conditions.<ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Spiraea+splendens ''Spiraea splendens''.] Native American Ethnobotany. University of Michigan, Dearborn.</ref>

===Other===
Native Americans found ''S. douglasii'' useful for making [[broom]]s and hanging seafood to cook.<ref>[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Spiraea+douglasii ''Spiraea douglasii''.] Native American Ethnobotany. University of Michigan, Dearborn.</ref>
[[File:Spiraea 'Grefsheim'.jpg|alt=Spiraea × cinerea 'Grefsheim'|thumb|''Spiraea'' × ''cinerea'' ''<nowiki/>'Grefsheim''' inflorescence]]
One detrimental issue with ''Spiraea'' species is that they are loved by [[Dermestidae|carpet beetle]]s; this can then encourage the pests into nearby houses. <ref>{{cite web |title=Carpet Beetles | Cleankill Pest Control |url=https://www.cleankill.co.uk/pests/carpet-beetles }}</ref>
